definition: Defiant means boldly refusing to obey or to submit to authority.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word defiant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know defiant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Ordered ashore ahead of the storm, the tugboat captain answered with one defiant blast of the horn and made her run anyway.
Uncooperative drags its feet and misses deadlines; defiant looks authority in the eye and says no.
Mutinous goes past defiant — the refusal has become an organized rising to seize control.

Rebellious rises against the whole system — the rules themselves, and the right of anyone to set them. Defiant can be far narrower: one order, boldly and openly refused, with no wish to overturn anything else. A teenager who rejects every house rule is rebellious; one who refuses a single curfew order to your face is defiant.

Insubordinate is the workplace and military version of refusal: a subordinate disobeying a direct superior, with rank on the org chart and a write-up to follow. Defiant is broader and bolder — anyone can be defiant toward any authority — and it stresses the open, chin-up manner of the refusal rather than the reporting line.

Defiant means boldly refusing to obey or to submit to authority.
The letter from the county was plain: the beloved treehouse violated setback rules and had thirty days to come down.
Alvarez read it on his porch, folded it once, and nailed it to the treehouse ladder.
Defiant to this day, he has attended every hearing with a 1932 deed in hand, and the treehouse has entered its fourth summer, unmoved.
Defiant is the exact word because it names bold refusal to obey — resistance aimed up, at an authority that expects to be obeyed.
Alvarez isn't merely stubborn about his own tastes; he is refusing an order, publicly, with the paperwork nailed where the county can see it.
Take away the order and you'd have persistence; against the order, it is defiance.
Defiant is refusal with its chin up, and it needs someone with the standing to give orders — a court, a county, a commander.
That need for an order separates it from this unit's contentious and pugnacious, which pick quarrels among equals.
If no order has been given and someone simply won't budge, the honest word is stubborn, not defiant.

At twelve, Amara Okafor was the youngest player ever seeded at the national chess open, and by all accounts the politest.
She thanked the arbiters, followed the clock rules to the second, and shook every opponent's hand.
But when officials ordered her to remove her grandmother's head-wrap before the televised final, she became quietly defiant.
She stated, on camera, that she would play exactly as she was or not at all, and sat down at the board still wearing it.
The federation backed down before the first pawn moved; the girl who obeyed every other rule had refused this one to their faces.
